title: Reading a pedigree chart
ask: Explain how you work out the mode of inheritance from a pedigree chart, how you assign genotypes, and how you find the chance of another affected child. Use an autosomal dominant family as your example: an affected father and an unaffected mother who have both affected and unaffected children. (5 marks)
hook: Emma's three questions: 1 does it SKIP a generation? (skips = recessive, never skips = dominant) 2 is there a GENDER difference? (even = autosomal, lopsided = X-linked) 3 who are the homozygous RECESSIVES? Label them first, then Punnett the parents.
steps: Read the chart: **squares = males**, **circles = females**, **shaded = affected**, half-shaded or dotted = **carrier**. Leave out people who **married in** when you check the generations.

**Dominant or recessive?** If the trait appears in **every generation** (does **not skip**) it is **dominant**; if it **skips a generation** (an affected child of two unaffected parents) it is **recessive**.
**Autosomal or X-linked?** Count affected **males vs females**: **equal = autosomal**, a clear difference = **sex-linked**. A **father passing it to his son** rules out X-linked.

X-linked checks: in **X-linked recessive**, fathers **cannot pass it to their sons** and affected mothers pass it to **all their sons**; in **X-linked dominant**, affected fathers pass it to **all their daughters**.

**Genotypes**: label the **homozygous recessives first** (bb, or XᵃY / XᵃXᵃ); everyone else has **at least one dominant allele**, and you work out the rest from their **parents and children**. Here the affected father must be **Bb**, because some of his children are unaffected (bb); the unaffected mother is **bb**.
**Chance**: draw a **Punnett square** of the parents' alleles. **Bb × bb** gives **2 Bb : 2 bb**, so each child has a **50%** chance of being affected.

short.hook: SKIP? (skips = recessive) · BOYS vs GIRLS? (even = autosomal) · RECESSIVES first · PUNNETT the parents: Bb × bb = 50%.

facts.t: A father passing it to his son **rules out X-linked**
X-linked dominant: affected fathers pass it to **all their daughters**
**2 Bb : 2 bb** = a **50%** chance for each child

traps: Say HOW you can tell (skips or not; males vs females; father to son). 'How can you tell?' carries its own marks in her question.
Father-to-son passing means it CANNOT be X-linked: a son gets his father's Y, not his X.
The chance is per child: 50% for EVERY pregnancy, not 'one in every two children'.
her: look at the following pedigree chart

mcq.q: On a pedigree chart, what does a shaded circle show?
mcq.why: Circles are females, squares are males; shaded means affected. A carrier is shown half-shaded or dotted.

mcq.q: A trait appears in every generation and never skips. It is most likely...
mcq.why: Her rule 1: if it does not skip a generation it is dominant; if it does, it is recessive.

mcq.q: Two unaffected parents have an affected child. The trait must be...
mcq.why: An affected child of two unaffected parents means both parents carried a hidden allele, so the trait is recessive. Her quiz key uses exactly this reason.

mcq.q: Equal numbers of affected males and females suggests the trait is...
mcq.why: Her rule 2: no difference between the sexes means autosomal; a clear difference means sex-linked.

mcq.q: An affected father has an affected son. Which pattern does this rule out?
mcq.why: A son inherits his father's Y, not his X, so a father cannot pass an X-linked trait to his son.

mcq.q: In X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected mother passes it to...
mcq.why: Her deck: affected mothers (XᵃXᵃ) ALWAYS pass it to their sons, because every son gets one of her two Xᵃ.

mcq.q: When assigning genotypes, whom should you label first?
mcq.why: Her rule 3: do the homozygous recessives first; everyone else must then have at least one dominant allele.

mcq.q: An affected father (dominant trait) has some unaffected children. His genotype is...
mcq.why: If he were BB every child would get B and be affected. Unaffected (bb) children mean he must carry a b: he is Bb.

mcq.q: What is the chance a Bb × bb couple has an affected child (dominant trait)?
mcq.why: The Punnett square gives 2 Bb (affected) and 2 bb (unaffected): 50% for each child.

title: Huntington's disease: a genetic disease
ask: Explain Huntington's disease as a genetic disease: its cause, how it damages the body, how it is inherited, and the chance of an affected child when one parent is Hh and the other is hh. (5 marks)
hook: Chromosome 4 → CAG stutters (36-120 repeats) → oversized huntingtin → toxic build-up in the brain → movement, thinking, memory. One H is enough (autosomal DOMINANT): Hh × hh = 50%.
steps: Huntington's is caused by a **mutated gene on chromosome 4**, an **autosome** (humans have **46 chromosomes: 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes**).
The mutation is a **copying error** during **DNA replication** (e.g. in sperm formation): the **CAG** base sequence is **repeated too many times**, **36-120 times** instead of the normal **10-35**.
The larger gene makes a larger, **abnormal huntingtin protein**, which is **toxic**, **builds up in the brain** and **damages brain cells**, especially those for **movement, thinking and memory**.
It is **autosomal dominant**: **one copy** of the mutated allele (**Hh**) is enough to cause the disease, and it can be inherited from **either parent**.
So there are **no healthy carriers**: anyone with an **H** allele develops the disease and only **hh** is unaffected; it shows in **every generation**.
**Hh × hh**: the Punnett square gives **2 Hh : 2 hh**, so each child has a **50%** chance of being affected.

short.hook: Chromosome 4 → CAG STUTTER → TOXIC protein in the brain → ONE H is enough: Hh × hh = 50%.

facts.t: It makes an **abnormal huntingtin protein**, which is **toxic**
It **builds up in the brain**: **movement, thinking and memory** suffer
**No healthy carriers**: Hh is affected, only hh is not

traps: DOMINANT: Hh is AFFECTED. Calling Hh a 'carrier' loses the mark (her deck asks: can a person be a healthy carrier? No).
Chromosome 4 is an AUTOSOME, not a sex chromosome.
It is a gene mutation (CAG repeats), not an extra or missing chromosome, so it is not aneuploidy.
src: Her 'HELP WITH MODULE 3 TOPICS' board (Huntington's: an abnormal gene on chromosome 4, humans have 46 chromosomes, 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes, autosomal dominant); her 2020 genetic disease Huntington's deck slides 4-13 (chromosome 4; copying inaccuracies during sperm formation; CAG repeats 10-35 normal vs 36-120; larger huntingtin is toxic and damages movement, thinking and memory cells; autosomal dominant, one copy needed, from either parent; the Punnett questions); her quiz keys (Hh; 50%).

mcq.why: Her slide: normally CAG repeats 10-35 times; in Huntington's it repeats 36 to 120 times.

title: Using a Punnett square
ask: Explain how a Punnett square is used to predict offspring. Work a Bb × Bb cross (brown eyes B dominant over blue b) and a codominant blood group cross (Iᴬi × Iᴮi). (4 marks)
hook: One parent across the top, one down the side, one letter from each into every box. Bb × Bb = 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes = 3 : 1 phenotypes. Iᴬi × Iᴮi = one of each blood group: A, B, AB, O.
steps: Genes come in pairs of **alleles**, **one from each parent**. A **Punnett square** shows **all the possible combinations** of the parents' alleles at **fertilisation**, so it predicts the **probability** of each offspring genotype.
Write one parent's alleles **across the top** and the other's **down the side**, then fill each box with **one allele from each parent**.
**Bb × Bb** gives **1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb**: **25% homozygous dominant, 50% heterozygous, 25% homozygous recessive**.
Phenotypes: BB and Bb both show the **dominant** trait, so **75% brown : 25% blue**; only **bb** shows the recessive trait.

**Codominance (ABO)**: **Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed** and **i** (O) is recessive. **Iᴬi × Iᴮi** gives **IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B) and ii (O)**, **25% each**, which is how four children can have four different blood groups.

short.hook: One parent ACROSS THE TOP, one DOWN THE SIDE, one letter from each into every box.

facts.t: **Alleles** come in pairs, **one from each parent**
It shows **all the possible combinations**: the **probability** of each
One parent **across the top**, the other **down the side**
Codominance: **Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed**; i (O) is recessive
Iᴬi × Iᴮi → **AB**, A, B and O, **25% each**

traps: Genotype (the letters: BB, Bb, bb) is not phenotype (what shows: brown or blue). Give both when asked.
Each box is a probability for EACH child, not a count of real children.
Heterozygous = Bb; homozygous = BB or bb.
src: Her 2026 PUNNETT SQUARES & Patterns of Inheritance deck slides 2-5 (alleles, one from each parent; Punnett square = all possible combinations; BB × bb, BB × Bb, Bb × Bb with genotype and phenotype percentages for brown and blue eyes), slides 8-10 (codominance, ABO; her IᴬI × ii and Iᴬi × Iᴮi worked squares: four children, four blood groups).

mcq.q: What does a Punnett square show?
mcq.a: Every possible allele combination in offspring
d: The actual number of children a couple will have
Which parent a disease first came from
The order of genes along a chromosome
mcq.why: Her deck: a Punnett square shows all possible combinations of alleles during fertilisation, so it gives probabilities.

mcq.q: How is a Punnett square filled in?
mcq.a: Each box takes one allele from each parent
d: Each box takes both alleles of one parent
Each box repeats the top row's allele
Each box shows one parent's phenotype
mcq.why: One parent's alleles go across the top and the other's down the side; each box combines one from each.

mcq.q: Bb × Bb: what proportion of offspring are heterozygous?
mcq.why: Two of the four boxes are Bb, so 50% are heterozygous.

mcq.q: Bb × Bb: what proportion are homozygous recessive?
mcq.why: Only one of the four boxes is bb.

mcq.q: Bb × Bb with brown (B) dominant: what share of children have brown eyes?
mcq.why: BB and both Bb boxes show brown: 3 of 4 = 75%. Only bb (25%) is blue.

mcq.q: Blood group AB shows both A and B antigens. This is...
mcq.why: Both alleles are fully expressed together: codominance. Her deck uses the ABO locus as the example.

mcq.q: Iᴬi × Iᴮi: what is the chance of a child with blood group O?
mcq.why: Her worked square: one box each of AB, A, B and O, so 25% each.

title: Patterns of inheritance
ask: Briefly explain these patterns of inheritance, with an example of each: codominance, incomplete dominance, polygenic inheritance and mitochondrial inheritance. (4 marks)
hook: CO = both show (AB blood). INCOMPLETE = a blend (sickle cell carrier). POLY = many genes, a smooth range (height). MITO = mum only, to all her kids, severity varies (bottleneck).
steps: **Codominance**: **both alleles are fully expressed** in the heterozygote, each making its own protein, e.g. **ABO blood groups**: Iᴬ and Iᴮ together give **AB**, with both A and B antigens.

**Incomplete dominance**: one allele **does not completely mask** the other, so the heterozygote is **intermediate**, e.g. **sickle cell**: the heterozygote has **both normal and sickle cells** (about a third of the haemoglobin abnormal) and more **resistance to malaria**.
**Polygenic inheritance**: **many genes** control one trait, giving a **continuous range** of variation (a **bell curve**), e.g. **height, skin colour, eye colour**.
**Mitochondrial inheritance**: genes in **mitochondrial DNA** are passed **only by the mother**, to **all her children** (sons and daughters); **fathers never pass it on**.

Mitochondrial disorders can appear in **both sexes in every generation**, but severity varies because of the **bottleneck effect**: symptoms appear once mutated mtDNA passes a **threshold** (often **60-90%**), e.g. **LHON**.

short.hook: CO = BOTH show (AB). INCOMPLETE = a BLEND (sickle cell). POLY = MANY genes (height). MITO = MUM only.

facts.t: e.g. **ABO blood groups**: A and B together give **AB**
One allele **does not completely mask** the other: **intermediate**
e.g. **sickle cell**: carriers have normal and sickle cells
**Many genes** control one trait: a **continuous range** (bell curve)
**Mitochondrial DNA** passes **only by the mother**, to **all her children**

traps: Codominance = BOTH shown fully (AB); incomplete dominance = a BLEND. Her quizzes pair them to catch you.
Her decks file sickle cell under INCOMPLETE dominance. Write it her way.
Mitochondrial: from the MOTHER to ALL her children, never from the father.

mcq.why: Her deck: incomplete dominance, e.g. sickle cell anaemia. ABO is her codominance example.

It sits on the X chromosome

mcq.why: Mitochondria come from the egg, so mtDNA is passed by the mother to all her children.

mcq.why: Her deck: fathers do not pass mitochondrial traits to their children.

title: Karyotypes and aneuploidy
ask: What is a human karyotype and how many chromosomes does it show? What is aneuploidy? Give two examples and explain how aneuploidy arises. (4 marks)
hook: 46 = 23 pairs = 22 pairs of autosomes + XX or XY. One too many (Down: three 21s, 47) or one too few (Turner: one X, 45) = aneuploidy, from pairs failing to separate in meiosis (non-disjunction).
steps: A **karyotype** is a picture of a cell's chromosomes (at **metaphase**) arranged into **numbered homologous pairs** by decreasing size: the complete **diploid** set.
Humans have **46 chromosomes = 23 pairs**: **22 pairs of autosomes** and **1 pair of sex chromosomes** (**XX** female, **XY** male).
**Aneuploidy** is an **abnormal number of chromosomes** in a cell (too many or too few).
Examples: **Down syndrome = trisomy 21** (**47** chromosomes, three copies of chromosome 21); **Turner syndrome = 45,X (XO)**, only one X. Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is another.

Aneuploidy is caused by **non-disjunction**: a chromosome pair or its chromatids **fail to separate** in **anaphase of meiosis** (I or II), so a **gamete** gets one too many or one too few, and so does the **zygote**.

short.hook: 46 = 23 PAIRS. ONE TOO MANY (Down, 47) or ONE TOO FEW (Turner, 45) = pairs failing to split in meiosis.

facts.t: A picture of the chromosomes in **numbered homologous pairs**
Pairs **fail to separate**, so a **gamete** gets one too many or few

traps: 46 chromosomes = 23 PAIRS = 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes. '23 autosomes' is wrong.
Non-disjunction happens in MEIOSIS, when gametes are made.

mcq.why: 22 pairs of autosomes plus 1 pair of sex chromosomes = 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes.

mcq.why: 46 (23 pairs). 23 is the number in a gamete; 47 is trisomy.

title: Detecting and treating genetic disease
ask: Explain some ways genetic abnormalities are detected, including genetic testing and fetal testing, and what genetic engineering and gene therapy are. (4 marks)
hook: LOOK (karyotype, CGH-array) → SAMPLE the baby early (CVS: placenta, 8-12 wk) or later (amnio: fluid, 14-20 wk) → CHANGE DNA (engineering: bacteria make insulin) → TREAT a patient (therapy: insert genes).
steps: **Genetic testing** reads a person's **DNA** (often from a **blood sample**) for genes or variants that cause disease, e.g. a **karyotype** (looking at the chromosomes) or a **molecular karyotype (CGH-array)**, which checks **thousands of positions** for missing or extra DNA.
**Amniocentesis**: **amniotic fluid** is removed at **14-20 weeks** and the **fetal cells** in it are examined for chromosomal and genetic disorders.
**Chorionic villus sampling (CVS)**: tissue is removed from the **placenta** at **8-12 weeks** and its cells are examined for chromosomal and genetic disorders.
**Genetic engineering** is the **deliberate alteration of DNA** to change an organism's genetic make-up, e.g. **bacteria altered to make insulin**.
**Gene therapy** is the **treatment of a genetic disease** by **inserting genetic material** into the patient's cells (carried in by a **vector**).

short.hook: LOOK (blood test, karyotype) → SAMPLE the baby (CVS early, amnio later) → CHANGE DNA (engineering) → TREAT (gene therapy).

facts.t: Both check the **fetal cells** for disorders
**Gene therapy**: **treatment of a genetic disease** by **inserting genetic material**

traps: CVS is EARLIER (8-12 weeks, placenta); amniocentesis is LATER (14-20 weeks, amniotic fluid).
Genetic ENGINEERING changes DNA (in any organism); gene THERAPY treats a patient's disease.
A karyotype shows chromosome NUMBER and shape. It cannot see a single-gene change like Huntington's.
